title: Generalization stability of the section component locus in a flat geometrically reduced family
statement: Let $g:P\to T$ be flat [def-weil-flat-morphism] and locally of finite presentation, quasi-compact and quasi-separated [def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation, def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions], with geometrically reduced fibres [def-pc-geometrically-irreducible], and let $\sigma:T\to P$ be a section [def-pc-scheme]. Put $C=\{p\in P\mid p$ lies in the connected component [def-weil-connected-scheme] of $\sigma(g(p))$ in the fibre $g^{-1}(\{g(p)\})$ [def-pc-scheme-fibre]$\}$. If $p$ specializes to $q$ and $q\in C$, then $p\in C$; equivalently, $C$ is stable under generalization.

source.place: Tag 055Q, lemma-connected-along-section-open-neighbourhood: generic-point and specialization argument for the relative section component

proof.text: Fix $p\leadsto q$ with $q\in C$. Apply [lem-trf-flat-pointed-noetherian-component-model] at $q$: flatness, finite presentation and the section are given, and the universal fibre hypothesis gives geometric reducedness at $g(q)$. Its affine open $V$ contains $g(q)$. Continuity gives $g(p)\leadsto g(q)$; an open containing a specialization contains its generalizations, so $p,q\in P_V$. The conclusion gives Noetherian $P_0,T_0$, flat finite presentation of $g_0$, $g_0\circ\sigma_0=\mathrm{id}_{T_0}$, reduced geometric fibre at $g_0(q_0)$, and $\rho^{-1}C(g_0,\sigma_0)=C\cap P_V$. Set $p_0=\rho(p)$, $q_0=\rho(q)$. The cartesian square gives $g_0(q_0)=b(g(q))$, identifying the reduced geometric fibre with the point needed for step 2. Continuity gives $p_0\leadsto q_0$; since $q\in C\cap P_V$, the equality gives $q_0\in C(g_0,\sigma_0)$. If $p_0=q_0$, then $p_0\in C(g_0,\sigma_0)$; evaluating the same inverse-image equality at $p\in P_V$ gives $p\in C$.

source.place: Tag 055Q, lemma-connected-along-section-open-neighbourhood, first paragraph: affine restriction, descent of family and section, eventual flatness, and the distinguished fibre

proof.text: For $p_0\ne q_0$, apply [lem-trf-flat-reduced-specialization-trait-data] to $g_0,\sigma_0,p_0,q_0$. Step 1 supplies Noetherian schemes, flat finite presentation, the section equation, $p_0\leadsto q_0$, $q_0\in C(g_0,\sigma_0)$ and reducedness of the geometric fibre at $g_0(q_0)$. Obtain $f:X\to S=\operatorname{Spec}R$, projection $r$, and sections $\sigma_R,\tau$ with $f\circ\sigma_R=f\circ\tau=\mathrm{id}_S$. The statement gives flat finite presentation of $f$, reduced $X_s$, $r(\tau(s))=q_0$, $r(\tau(\eta))=p_0$, and $C(f,\sigma_R)=r^{-1}C(g_0,\sigma_0)$. Evaluating the last identity at $\tau(s)$ gives $\tau(s)\in C(f,\sigma_R)$. As $f(\tau(s))=s$, this means $\tau(s)$ is in the component of $\sigma_R(s)$ in $f^{-1}(\{s\})$, exactly the closed-component hypothesis for step 3.

source.place: Tag 055Q, lemma-connected-along-section-open-neighbourhood, second paragraph: specialization trait, graph section and reduced closed fibre

proof.text: Apply [lem-trf-flat-trait-two-section-connected-open] to $f,\sigma_R,\tau$: step 2 supplies the DVR, flat finite presentation, reduced closed fibre, both section equations and the common closed-fibre component. Obtain the connected nonempty generic fibre $W_\eta$, with both generic section points. Its continuous image in $f^{-1}(\{\eta\})$ is connected: a separation of the image would pull back to a separation of $W_\eta$. This image contains $\sigma_R(\eta)$ and $\tau(\eta)$, so maximality of the component through $\sigma_R(\eta)$ puts $\tau(\eta)$ in that component. Since $f(\tau(\eta))=\eta$ by the section equation, this says $\tau(\eta)\in C(f,\sigma_R)$.

source.place: Tag 055Q, lemma-connected-along-section-open-neighbourhood, last paragraph: remove other closed-fibre components, retain a connected open, apply the connected-generic-fibre theorem

proof.text: By [lem-trf-flat-reduced-specialization-trait-data], $C(f,\sigma_R)=r^{-1}C(g_0,\sigma_0)$ and $r(\tau(\eta))=p_0$; hence $p_0\in C(g_0,\sigma_0)$. Finally [lem-trf-flat-pointed-noetherian-component-model] gives $\rho^{-1}C(g_0,\sigma_0)=C\cap P_V$. Evaluating at $p\in P_V$, with $\rho(p)=p_0$, yields $p\in C\cap P_V$, hence $p\in C$. Together with step 1's equality case, this proves generalization stability.
